articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.
These designations aim to disrupt financial networks supporting illicit activities globally, reinforcing the U.S. commitment to combating international drug trafficking and terrorism financing.
Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the implications for U.S. persons, are available in the official release.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: OFAC released an update on November 9, 2026, concerning designations related to Iran. This action is part of ongoing efforts to exert economic pressure on the Iranian regime.
The update includes additional individuals and entities, further restricting Iran's access to the international financial system and targeting its illicit activities.
This move aligns with broader U.S. policy to counter Iran's proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities and ballistic missile program.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026, as part of its strategy to cripple financial networks sustaining the Iranian regime.
These designations target entities and individuals involved in supporting Iran's illicit activities, including those related to its nuclear and missile programs.
The U.S. Department of State also highlighted these sanctions as part of efforts to disrupt Iranian financial networks.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations; Cuba Designations; Publishes Cuba-related Determination
body: OFAC announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new Cuba designations.
The Cuba-related actions include designating entities and individuals involved in crude oil shipping networks, state-owned entities, and Chinese military suppliers.

Additionally, OFAC issued a determination extending Executive Order 14404 to four new sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine, allowing for future sanctions on foreign persons operating in these areas.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-related Designations, Updates Listings, Publishes Alert, and Amends Venezuela-related General License
body: On November 4, 2026, OFAC announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing listings. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' targeting Iran's shadow fleet and aviation support networks.
An Iran-related OFAC Alert was also published, specifically addressing the Iranian Shadow Fleet's reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion.
Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question, providing updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: On October 29, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License.
This amendment provides updated authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy.
The specifics of the amended license are detailed in the official publication and should be reviewed by all relevant parties.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Announces North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo-related Designations
body: OFAC announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
These actions aim to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses in these regions, reinforcing international efforts to promote stability and accountability.
The designations underscore the U.S. commitment to addressing threats posed by these regimes and their associates.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs Regarding Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: On October 26, 2026, OFAC issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.
These amendments provide updated guidance and clarifications for financial institutions and other U.S. persons on their obligations under OFAC regulations.
The updated FAQs are crucial for ensuring compliance with sanctions programs and proper reporting procedures.

articles.headline: UK Adds 20 Entities to Russia Sanctions List, Imposes Transport Sanctions
body: On November 12, 2026, the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List, adding 20 entities and one variation under the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019.
These additions include asset freezes, trust services sanctions, director disqualification sanctions, and transport sanctions.

The transport sanctions prohibit ships and aircraft owned, controlled, chartered, or operated by designated persons from entering UK ports or airspace, and also restrict technical assistance related to such vessels.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,529,685
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to pay $1,529,685.
This settlement resolves potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
The details of the violations and the factors considered in determining the settlement amount are outlined in OFAC's enforcement release.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 in OFAC Settlement for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs.
The violations involved processing payments for blocked banks, failing to update watchlists, and mishandling accounts associated with blocked persons.
OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to the significant settlement amount.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

The violations stemmed from facilitating the importation of a sugar packet-filling machine from a sanctioned Chinese supplier, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which had changed its name after designation.

OFAC found that Pegasus failed to adequately screen information it possessed and did not fully respond to an administrative subpoena, highlighting the importance of thorough screening and complete subpoena responses.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $1,427,230 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: An individual has settled with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for a civil penalty of $1,427,230.
This penalty addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
The specific details of the individual's violations are typically outlined in the enforcement release associated with the settlement.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination based on the nature of the violations and the company's cooperation.
Further information regarding the specific violations is typically provided in the official enforcement release.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 in OFAC Settlement
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has settled with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $1,050,000.
This payment resolves potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs.
The enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued focus on compliance across various industries.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Settles with OFAC for $275,000,000 Over Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-headquartered multinational company, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions regulations.
The violations involved causing U.S. financial institutions to process approximately $192 million in payments for Iranian-origin liquid petroleum gas (LPG) between November 2023 and June 2025.

OFAC deemed the violations egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing numerous red flags that AEL either missed or dismissed without adequate investigation, including warnings about Iranian-origin cargo and commercially implausible pricing.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,110,661 for Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle its potential civil liability for 481 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs.

For nearly a year, from June 2021 to June 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine, enabling them to execute securities-related transactions.

The settlement reflects OFAC's determination that the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, and highlights the importance for financial institutions to ensure compliance tools are adequately implemented and functioning.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $3,777,000 in OFAC Civil Penalty for Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle potential civil liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.
The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021, underscoring OFAC's focus on enforcing sanctions against individuals, even those residing outside the United States.
This significant penalty reflects the seriousness of the violations and OFAC's commitment to preventing illicit financial activities that undermine U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Settles with OFAC for $1,720,000 Over Counternarcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a Florida-based school and athletic training facility, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 89 apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.
Over a five-year period, IMG Academy repeatedly transacted with two individuals designated under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.

The settlement highlights OFAC's expectation that institutions across various sectors, including academic institutions with international student bodies, implement effective, risk-based controls to prevent sanctions violations.

articles.headline: Democrats Gain Control of Congress in 2026 Midterm Elections, Rebuking Trump
body: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections resulted in a significant shift towards the Democrats, who gained control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
This outcome is widely seen as a direct repudiation of President Donald Trump and his party's policies, with Democrats securing several surprise upsets.

The Associated Press reported that the Democrats are now poised to launch a 100-day agenda focused on lowering the costs of gas, groceries, and healthcare, and initiating extensive oversight and investigations into the Trump administration.

articles.headline: U.S. to Halt $4 Billion Aid to Israel in 2027, Shift to Arms Sales
body: President Donald Trump announced on November 3, 2026, that the U.S. will cease providing $4 billion in annual aid to Israel starting in 2027, opting instead to sell arms to its Middle East ally.
Trump stated that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approached him with the idea, and they have been discussing it for several years, citing that Israel no longer needs the aid.
Leaders in Israel's opposition bloc have expressed concerns that ending U.S. military aid would deliver a 'severe blow to Israel's security'.

articles.headline: Greenland Approves Security Deal with Denmark and U.S. Amid Trump Pressure
body: Greenlandic lawmakers have approved a security agreement with Denmark and the United States aimed at strengthening security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
This decision follows months of pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, who had sought greater control over the semi-autonomous territory of a NATO ally.

The trilateral deal will allow for an increased U.S. military presence in Greenland while maintaining the island under Danish control, easing tensions over Trump's previous calls for Greenland to become part of the United States.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
